0._section_summary: This abstract reports the development of the Caregiver Eating Messages Scale and presents results from two studies (Ns = 238, 288) indicating two factors (restrictive/critical messages and pressure to eat). Findings indicate both factors were positively related to women's BMI and restrictive/critical messages were positively related to men's BMI; restrictive/critical messages predicted lower perceived familial body acceptance, lower intuitive eating, higher perceived familial pressure to be lean, and higher disordered eating, and uniquely predicted men's body appreciation. The abstract explicitly states there were two studies but provides no sample demographics, survey method, exact BMI means, or correlation coefficients.

3._section_summary: This Measures section describes instruments used in the study, including a newly developed Caregiver Eating Messages Scale (CEMS) that was piloted with 43 college students, the Family subscale of the Body Acceptance by Others Scale (BAOS) for perceived familial acceptance, the 13-item Body Appreciation Scale (BAS) for body appreciation, the Intuitive Eating Scale (IES), and computation of BMI from self-reported height and weight. 4.evidence_source: The significance of Bartlett's test of sphericity, x2 (153, N = 238) = 1626.91, p < .001, and the size of the Kaiser–Meyer– Oklin measure of sampling adequacy = .78, revealed that the CEMS had adequate common variance for factor analysis (Tabachnick & Fidell, 2001).
4._section_summary: This section reports an exploratory factor analysis of the 15-item CEMS conducted on a sample of N = 238. Parallel analysis retained two factors (Pressure to Eat Messages and Restrictive and Critical Messages) after retaining 10 items; the two factors had eigenvalues of 3.37 and 2.66 and accounted for 33.69% and 26.64% of the variance, respectively. The final CEMS (10 items) used in remaining analyses is presented in Appendix A.

5.evidence_source: Notes: N = 238. Data from women (n = 160) are presented below the diagonal, whereas data from men (n = 78) are presented above the diagonal. We evaluated the test–retest reliability of the CEMS scores over a 4-week period with a subsample of 18 young adult students (56% women, 44% men, M age = 20.65, SD = 2.78, 94% Caucasian) who volunteered to participate in a follow-up study without incentive.
5._section_summary: This section reports reliability analyses, sample sizes, and multigroup structural modeling for a single study (N = 238; women n = 160, men n = 78), including a 4-week test–retest subsample of 18 young adult students (M age = 20.65; 94% Caucasian). 13._section_summary: This section describes the development and validation of the Caregiver Eating Messages Scale (CEMS), which assesses perceptions of caregivers' restrictive/critical and pressure-to-eat messages. Experts reviewed items, and a psychometric investigation found a two-factor structure with internally consistent and stable scores over a 4-week period.

14.evidence_source: Outside of this difference, this study suggests that the processes to which perceived restrictive/critical caregiver eating messages are associated with perceptions of family members' attitudes toward their bodies and their eating behaviors may be similar for adult men and women.
14._section_summary: The section reports results from a single (unnamed) study of young adults indicating that perceived restrictive/critical caregiver eating messages were negatively related to perceived familial body acceptance, body appreciation, and intuitive eating, and positively related to family pressure to be lean, body dissatisfaction, disordered eating, and BMI. A gender difference was identified: for men restrictive/critical messages were uniquely associated with lower body appreciation, whereas for women this relationship was fully accounted for by perceived familial body acceptance; otherwise the processes were similar across genders.

15.evidence_source: The text repeatedly refers to "this study" (singular), e.g., "Despite its contributions, this study's limitations need to be addressed." indicating a single study.
15._section_summary: This limitations section notes reliance on self-report measures and retrospective recall, a homogeneous sample of predominantly White, young adult, middle-class first-year college students, and measurement issues (e.g., use of the EDI-2 Body Dissatisfaction subscale and brief subscales of BAOS/PSPS). It calls for future research using multiple informants, more diverse samples, time-specific assessments of caregiver eating messages, validation of the CEMS in clinical populations, and exploration of caregiver characteristics and adaptive eating messages.
